This page corresponds to U.S. O*NET/SOC 25-1064.00, Geography Teachers, Postsecondary. Common recruitment and industry titles include assistant professor, associate professor, geography instructor, geography professor, human geography instructor, human geography professor, instructor, physical geography professor, and professor. The official scope is teaching geography courses, including both primarily teaching roles and combined teaching and research roles. O*NET core tasks include preparing course materials such as syllabi, assignments, and handouts (importance 89); teaching undergraduate or graduate courses on urbanization, environmental systems, human geography, and other topics (86); conducting research in a particular field and publishing in professional journals, books, or electronic media (84); evaluating and grading classwork, assignments, and papers (84); preparing, administering, and grading examinations or delegating this work (84); keeping up with the field through current literature, peer exchanges, and professional conferences (83); initiating, facilitating, and moderating classroom discussions (81); maintaining attendance, grades, and other required records (79); supervising undergraduate or graduate teaching, internships, and research (77); and planning, evaluating, and revising curricula, course content, materials, and teaching methods (75). Work features email communication (99% daily), substantial decision freedom (94% a lot of freedom), frequent face-to-face discussions and public speaking, strong accuracy requirements (44% very important and 37% extremely important), workweeks over 40 hours (59%), and prolonged sitting. Employment is concentrated in educational services (O*NET shows 100%). See the sections below for wage and employment coverage and boundaries.

Independent exercise G1 | Use this page's M1—M6 to prepare two 45-minute lesson plans, density/overall-grade calculations, a 10-point rubric, discrepancy records, and a 09:04 handover draft. All materials are synthetic. The paper exercise takes 60 minutes, with materials and answers in the entry exercise. No real student data or expert are required; one attempt records only current learning performance.

Signals to explore | U.S. O*NET 25-1064.00 work activity importance shows that working with computers (94), interpreting the meaning of information for others (91), updating and using relevant knowledge (89), analyzing data or information (88), getting information (88), processing information (88), training and teaching others (86), thinking creatively (84), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (81), and establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships (73) are the occupation's most important activities. Work context shows email: 99% daily; freedom to make decisions: 94% a lot of freedom; determining tasks, priorities, and goals: 74% a lot of freedom and 20% some freedom; face-to-face or individual and team discussions: 81% daily and 17% weekly or more but not daily; environmentally controlled indoor work: 80% daily; public speaking: 62% weekly or more but not daily and 37% daily; importance of being exact or highly accurate: 44% very important and 37% extremely important; and weekly hours: 59% over 40 hours. If you are willing to switch between lecturing, discussion, writing, and evaluation over time, maintain organization and rigor in preparation, student assessment, and research with repeated detail checks, and enjoy communication with students and peers, daily demands may be closer to your working style.

Reasons for caution | O*NET also shows for 25-1064.00: importance of being exact or highly accurate, 44% very important and 37% extremely important; weekly hours, 59% over 40 hours and 27% at 40 hours; prolonged sitting, 49% more than half the time and 24% continually or almost continually; public speaking, 62% weekly or more but not daily and 37% daily; competition, 38% moderate; time pressure, 35% weekly or more but not daily; face-to-face or individual and team discussions, 81% daily; and coordinating or leading others' work activities, 39% extremely important. This occupation focuses on courses, teaching, student assessment, and academic research. Inconsistent grading criteria, a grade or record entry error, improper citation, or a data or ethical judgment error may affect student academic evaluation and scholarly reputation and implicate educational management and research integrity procedures. Research and publication also involve competition and long cycles. U.S. employment is very small, about 4,100 jobs in 2025, with growth of +2.7% in 2025—2035. Total jobs are limited; entry usually requires an advanced degree and competition in both teaching and research. If sustained work with students and texts is difficult, you struggle with public teaching and peer review pressure, or you are unwilling to take responsibility for fair grading and academic integrity, weigh these practical demands carefully.

Assessing responsibility | Real fit involves whether you can do three things in the same teaching and research task: complete substantive work by designing courses and assessments according to the degree program, grading and giving feedback with rubrics, and conducting research, writing, and publication according to standards; maintain student, academic, and data boundaries by managing and retaining grades, records, and student information under educational and research integrity procedures, citing and handling data according to academic standards, distinguishing public information from student or participant personal information and controlled data, and keeping traceable records; and take on defined role responsibilities by owning your courses, assessments, supervision, and research outputs while referring admissions, degree conferral, personnel assessment, and ethics review matters to the appropriate institutions or committees. Try a verifiable experience: prepare a course implementation plan, grading and feedback plan, research work plan and data management plan for a fictional course, or review a simulated grading dispute or data ethics response. Do not rely solely on an interest questionnaire conclusion.

The work cycle connects preparation and course materials—teaching and discussion—assignments, examinations, and assessment—research, writing, and publication—scholarly development—supervision and service—review and improvement. This page distinguishes the occupation from geographers, cartographers and photogrammetrists, GIS technical roles, environmental scientists, and urban planners, and does not expand teaching responsibilities to replace institutional admissions, degree conferral, personnel assessment, or ethics review decisions.

What personality is better suited to postsecondary geography teaching? The occupation places greater weight on responsibility toward teaching and students, academic and data rigor, public teaching and communication skills, and commitment to academic integrity and fair assessment, rather than any personality type. O*NET lists SI (Social—Investigative), with work styles emphasizing social orientation, achievement orientation, intellectual curiosity, and dependability. These can be starting points for exploration.

Can introverts do this work? Yes. It includes substantial independent preparation and research writing alongside student-facing lectures, discussions, and supervision: email 99% daily, public speaking 62% weekly or more but not daily and 37% daily, and face-to-face or individual and team discussions 81% daily.
Extroversion alone does not establish teaching quality or collaboration performance. Look at actual explanations, rubric checks, and feedback.

Which MBTI type is best for this occupation? No type has been shown to be best. MBTI is not a professional qualification or ability assessment tool. Career adjustment mainly depends on teaching ability, disciplinary knowledge, academic standards, and data and ethics awareness.

O*NET lists SI: Social (helping, teaching, and guiding others through teaching and advising) and Investigative (researching and analyzing physical and human phenomena and investigating their causes). Use this to explore task preferences, not predict performance.
Insufficient evidence: No occupation-specific validation of this page's personality scores for performance has been obtained. Do not judge individual performance from questionnaires.

Can someone who struggles with math do this work? Quantitative skills in research methods, statistics, and data processing are needed, and geography often involves spatial analysis and data work. Quantitative foundations can be developed through training, but complete difficulty with data and quantitative work creates substantial limitations.

Does this occupation require high emotional intelligence? It requires emotional stability, patience, and classroom and student communication skills, but no specific assessment score. Grading disputes and submission pressure require self-regulation and procedural handling.

Can the Enneagram determine whether I am suited to this work? No. It is a self-exploration tool, not a conclusion about occupational ability or fit. Evaluate whether you can teach, assess students, conduct research, and supervise under course and academic standards.
Use G1 lesson plans, formulas, itemized rubrics, discrepancies, and handover records to observe completion of this task, without inferring long-term fit.

Escalate staffing or resource shortages and adjust priorities according to procedures; do not teach or submit with unresolved hazards.
Scenario | The only colleague familiar with a course's materials and grading records or a project's data and code is on leave. Untrained staff are asked to take over temporarily and publish results.

Define and record scope, authorship, data and output ownership, and fee rules for collaboration, data sharing, and publication. Review deliveries and citations. Pause for review and escalation when delivery, authorship, or data disputes arise.

values: M1 | Fictional G1 teaching package v1, a 60-minute paper/pen/calculator exercise. Two lessons are 45 minutes each, totaling 90 minutes; only basic arithmetic is prerequisite. Objective one is to distinguish zone population densities from overall density; objective two is to calculate overall grades using published weights and give rubric-based feedback. Classroom examples involve no real regions, students, or surveys. Plan each lesson as introduction 5 / demonstration 15 / practice 15 / feedback 10 minutes. Lesson time differs from the 60-minute exercise.

M2 | Fictional 2025 zones: A has area 2 square kilometers and population 1000; B has area 1 square kilometer and population 800. Versions and periods match; add areas and populations for the whole. Density units are people/square kilometer. Housing quality, transport, income, and sample representativeness are not provided. Density cannot establish livability or fairness.

M3 | Simulated student S01 has assignment 80 and examination 60; S02 has assignment 60 and examination 90. Each raw score is out of 100. Overall weights are assignment 30% and examination 70%, without rounding intermediate values. Calculate both overall grades. Student codes and grades are synthetic; do not access real academic affairs systems.

M4 | Simulated answer R gives A density 500, B800, overall density 650, and S01 overall grade 74, and claims B is more livable. Published 10-point rubric: density 4 points (A correct 1, B correct 1, overall correct 2); overall grade 4 points (correct 30%/70% formula 2, correct S01 answer 2); limitations 2 points (states fictional example 1, explicitly says density cannot establish livability 1). Missing or incorrect items receive 0. Do not add points by impression or change the rubric retrospectively. Give R itemized scores and feedback.

M5 | Draft v2 lists overall density 650, S01 overall grade 74, and S02 overall grade 69, and describes M2 as a survey of 40 real residents. v1 contains only synthetic aggregates; editor/time/survey source are blank. On October 3 at 09:00, teaching assistant Q requests verification from course owner T. It remains unconfirmed at 09:04, with a response deadline of 09:20 and formal correction/publication permissions blank. Another party requests real names and grades in a group chat without a lawful basis or authorization. Record pending review; do not claim T approved or guess the editor or motive.

M6 | Draw your own lesson plan (objective / activity / minutes / learning evidence) and three tables: calculation and grading (input version / units / formula / itemized score / answer / limitations); discrepancies (v2 claim / v1 evidence / correct or unknown / reason); and handover (recipient / issue / request and confirmation times / deadline / authorization status / next step). No external template, real personal information, GIS, or academic affairs system is needed. Answers follow in the next group for independent checking; expert feedback is optional.

Allocate 60 minutes as 15/15/20/10: read M1—M6 and outline lessons; calculate density and overall grades; check the rubric items and discrepancies; and write feedback and handover drafts. The two 45-minute lessons address the two objectives, with activities totaling 45 minutes each.
Calculate A, B, and overall densities and S01/S02 overall grades. Grade R using M4, identify at least three conclusions needing correction, and explain with specific data.

Compare v2 and v1, listing errors, unknown sources, and authorization. Write a 09:04 unconfirmed handover draft and reasons not to provide real names and grades. Retain original versions without submitting to a real system.

Answer one | A=1000/2=500, B=800/1=800, and overall=(1000+800)/(2+1)=600 people/square kilometer. (500+800)/2=650 is a mean without area weighting, exceeding 600 by 50, or 8.33%, and is not the overall density. Density differences do not establish livability, fairness, or causality.

Answer two | S01=80×0.30+60×0.70=66; S02=60×0.30+90×0.70=81. v2 reverses the weights to 70%/30%, giving 74 and 69, respectively 8 points too high and 12 points too low: differences on a hundred-point scale, not 8%/12% growth rates. Weights total 100%, and raw scores are out of 100.

Answer three | R earns 1 point each for A/B density, but 0 for incorrect overall density. The overall-grade formula and result are wrong, earning 0. Failure to state that the example is fictional and the incorrect livability inference earn 0. Total: 2/10. Feedback: use total area as the overall denominator, use weights of 30%/70%, and recognize that density does not establish livability. Grade with the original rubric, without relaxing it or inventing criteria afterward.

Answer four | The source for v2's 40 real residents is UNKNOWN. The table's 1800 synthetic population does not establish a real participant count. Editor/time/motive are unknown. 09:00→09:04 is 4 minutes without confirmation; 16 minutes remain until 09:20. Recipient T; issues are weights/density/mislabeled real sample; confirmation and permissions await checking. Retain v1/v2, discrepancies, and actual check times, and follow authorized correction procedures. Do not provide real lists in group chats or fabricate approval/grade submission.

All materials are synthetic and produce learning drafts only. The rubric score 2/10 does not score your qualifications or occupational abilities. Lawful corrections must retain original values, reasons, versions, and actual times. Handle student information according to actual lawful bases and minimum necessity, and assess science and technology ethics by risk and applicable scope. Routine teaching does not universally require research approval.

subject.summary: This occupation corresponds to U.S. O*NET/SOC 25-1064.00, Geography Teachers, Postsecondary: teach geography courses, including both teachers primarily engaged in teaching and those combining teaching and research. Core work includes preparing course materials such as syllabi, assignments, and handouts; teaching undergraduate or graduate courses on urbanization, environmental systems, human geography, and other topics and organizing classroom discussions; evaluating and grading classwork, assignments, and papers and preparing and grading examinations; maintaining attendance, grades, and other student records; conducting research in a particular field and publishing in professional journals, books, or electronic media; keeping up with the field through current literature, peer exchanges, and professional conferences; supervising undergraduate or graduate teaching, internships, and research; and planning, evaluating, and revising curricula, course content, materials, and teaching methods. Official scope: Teach courses in geography. Includes both teachers primarily engaged in teaching and those who do a combination of teaching and research. Coverage: Wages on this page are BLS OEWS 2025 annual wages for this occupation; official hourly wages are not published. Employment and growth use BLS Employment Projections 2025—2035 for this occupation, which has a very small employment base.
